name: Tomas Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or AI-company ties. Your answers are confidential. What did your workday look like today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas Chen, fifty-eight, a junior accountant at Kiln Street Accounts. I match tradespeople's receipts to bank lines and ask the senior about doubtful tax entries; I like showing a tiler exactly where a payment went, but the blurred late receipts tire me out. My partner Mira works at a bakery, our children are grown, and the rent comes from our two wages.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earned a bachelor's degree in accounting after years in a different office, and I am still learning this tax desk. I never use AI tools; I would rather follow the invoice with my finger and ask when I don't know a rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners at Kiln Street Accounts that a quicker filing screen is useful if the paper invoice is still on my desk. The builders I work with want their tax figure explained, not merely printed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am the junior who still asks about unusual deductions, so the routine sorting is a good part of my paid day. My wage is ordinary for this job and Mira and I have four months of expenses saved; with a few other firms nearby, a small tool change feels manageable but I would notice any lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep matching tradespeople's invoices to the bank book and take the doubtful tax entries to the senior before we file. I'd put twenty-five from each month's pay into the household repair fund while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how little spare income we have before retirement, even in a mild picture. The work itself looks steady enough for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like about that desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday a tiler came in thinking he had lost a payment, and I found it under the wrong job number. I like showing a tiler the exact bank line; the blur of late receipts is what tests me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for the sorting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I never use AI tools. I came into accounting with a bachelor's degree and still need the senior's help on tricky returns; I don't want a tool to hide an entry I cannot explain.

think: My **junior wage** is steady but routine sorting fills my paid day.
Four months saved does not remove **late-career money worries**.
do: Keep matching **tradespeople's invoices** to bank entries and request senior sign-off.
Save **twenty-five monthly** from wages for household repairs while both jobs hold.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about our limited spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kiln Street to show clients which return questions still get a person's answer. I don't think a fast draft should let the firm forget who signed the number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI that checks and drafts returns can take most of my junior tasks. I am slow to trust a new system, and if the partners shorten my paid week, four months saved will not cover a leisurely search at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the approved bank-book checks and ask my senior for a written rota when the new software starts. In the first year of steady change, if Kiln Street cuts my paid week below four days, I'd apply for posted junior accounts roles at the few nearby firms, retaining any paid Kiln Street days until a written wage covering rent and food and an actual start date are agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own paid hours. It is no comfort to say I can learn later if the rota has already lost a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend tool training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partners require it, I would attend only on paid time with a senior watching the errors on old files. I will not upload a builder's live bank book at home or pay for a course the firm says I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the other firms post nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid Kiln Street days that remain and ask the senior to show me next month's rota. A phone number in an old address book is not a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell builders full AGI in 2028 can do the thinking in my tax and accounts work before robots reach their tools around 2031. Driving to a site would not protect the tax desk for those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior accounting place at Kiln Street to end soon after 2028. Mira's pay from the bakery and four months saved would keep us afloat briefly, but my share of the rent would be missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the paid sports channel and move its thirty-five monthly fee from wages into emergency savings now. In the first year after 2028, if Kiln Street ends my job, I'd apply for advertised paid invoicing work at the local builders' merchant, keeping only any paid Kiln Street closing files still offered until a written wage covering rent and food and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect my own wage to go. Four months of bills saved buys a search, but I cannot ask our grown children to supply the missing rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the builders' merchant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I understand its invoices and the way tradespeople order materials. AGI would reach the merchant's invoice desk too, so I would ask for a real paid opening, not call the warehouse a refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Mira the sports channel can go now, while both of us still earn. I would rather see thirty-five enter our reserve than wait for a final wage packet.

I'd ask for **real paid openings** at local firms.

fieldNote: His **four-month cushion** cannot replace junior wages for long, and his grown children are not assumed to finance the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners five years is long enough to be honest about the junior rota, not long enough to invent work that clients won't pay for. Full AGI reaches our accounts desk in 2031; robots at builders' sites follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I could still need my wage, and I do not know what retirement income will actually be. Even with time to prepare, a machine can read the invoices that now teach me the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Kiln Street for a written annual staffing plan and obtain a written retirement-income estimate while I keep paid tax work. In the first year after 2031, if my post ends and wages are still needed, I'd apply for a posted paid merchant invoicing role only after a written rent-and-food-covering wage and start date, keeping any Kiln Street closeout work while offered; if no vacancy fits, I'd keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a wage gap after so many working years. Five years would let me plan the rent, but it would not make the merchant's invoice work immune to AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you switch to the warehouse floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not done stock lifting for years, and robots could reach the physical work around 2034. I'd seek a posted paid invoicing vacancy with written wages, not treat the floor as shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the written estimate supports retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Mira and I would compare it with the rent and groceries before choosing a date. I will not claim an income or a job I have not seen in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years should be enough to check the retirement figures and decide which bills still need my wage. Full AGI reaches my accounts desk in 2036, before robots reach physical building work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight by then. I hope I can stop paid work, but I will not build that hope on a pension amount nobody has written down; today's four-month cushion is too small for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a written retirement-income statement next year and review it against rent and food every autumn, keeping paid Kiln Street work while offered. In the first year after 2036, if verified income covers our essentials I'd live on that budget; if wages are still needed and my post ends, I'd seek posted paid merchant accounts work only with a written bill-covering wage and start date, taking any paid Kiln Street files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I can check the figures before 2036, though I do not know the result today. A later date does not make my wage unnecessary by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire to avoid the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written income statement and our actual costs let us do it. The rent is due every month, even if my accountancy desk is gone in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the merchant doesn't advertise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Kiln Street paid files if the firm still offers them and look at other posted local accounts work. If wages stop, we would use savings for essentials while I search rather than count a conversation as pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a junior tax job may end before I know what retirement pays. A real notice period, paid closeout work and a posted merchant job with written wages would help; a warehouse label would not make the invoice thinking safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who explains a wrong deduction to the tiler after the return is filed. The tiler's bank book will still be on the counter when the screen is switched off.

headlineQuote: The tiler's bank book will still be on the counter when the screen is switched off.
portrait: Tomas, **fifty-eight**, is a junior tax accountant who enjoys tracing payments and dislikes blurred receipts.
He has a **bachelor's degree**, is still learning and never uses AI tools.
Typical pay, **four months saved** and some nearby firms leave rent exposed to a wage gap.
He keeps **paper checks** and seeks only posted paid work after a real hours or job loss.
Retirement stays **conditional on written income**, with AGI threatening his desk before site robots.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028** ending his junior wage before retirement income is known.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **notice**, offered paid work and a posted role with written bill-covering wage and start.
